passage:
For most of the last century, botanists described a plant's roots with a single verb: roots absorb. Water moved into the root, up the stem, and out through the leaves, and the direction of travel was assumed never to reverse. The desert shrub that herders call greasebush was studied for decades under that assumption, and nothing in its behaviour seemed to require another.

The assumption began to give way when a research team injected a harmless chemical marker into the deep, damp soil beneath a stand of greasebush and then sampled the shallow soil, and the seedlings rooted in it, every few days for six weeks. The marker turned up where it had no business being: in the top ten centimetres of soil, which had received no rain at all, and in the tissue of small seedlings as far as 1.4 metres from the nearest adult shrub. Repeated measurement showed that the shrubs drew water upward all night and released roughly a quarter of it back into the dry surface soil, from which the sun took it by midmorning. In the most closely monitored season the figure was 27 percent.

Why a plant in a place defined by scarcity should give water away is still argued. One group of researchers treats the seedlings as the point. Shaded and watered by their elders, the young survive, and since a seedling near an adult is usually that adult's own offspring, the parent's loss is the lineage's gain. A second group finds this unnecessary. A shrub's finest roots, they observe, lie in the surface soil, where the nutrients are; those roots die within days in dry ground and are costly to regrow. Dampening the surface keeps them alive and keeps the nutrients moving. On this reading the seedlings are merely standing in a puddle that was never meant for them.

The two accounts do not predict the same world. If the water is meant for kin, a shrub ringed by strangers should release less of it. That experiment has not yet been done.

passage:
The song a male sparrow sings is not invented. He learns it, during a few weeks of his first summer, from the adults within earshot, and the result is a local dialect: two valleys an hour’s walk apart can hold populations whose songs a practised ear separates at once. Because the learning window closes and the song then holds steady for life, a dialect was long treated as a fixed label — useful to researchers precisely because it could not change.

A programme of translocation put that usefulness to the test. To rebuild a population lost to a fire, fifty-one adult males were caught in one valley and released in another forty kilometres away, whose dialect differed in the placement of a single trill. The birds were recorded weekly. Within one breeding season thirty-eight of the fifty-one were singing the trill in its new position. The remaining thirteen never altered a note.

The obvious reading is that the window does not close after all, and that an adult sparrow can learn. A second reading has proved harder to dismiss. Young males, it turns out, memorise far more song than they ever perform: recordings made in a bird’s first summer catch fragments of neighbouring dialects that drop out of the repertoire before the first breeding season and were assumed to have been discarded. If those fragments are stored rather than discarded, the translocated males were not learning in adulthood but retrieving something learned on schedule and never used. The thirteen holdouts would then be the birds that had never happened to hear the second dialect as juveniles.

Choosing between the two readings would require knowing what each bird heard in its first summer, and for a wild-caught adult that is unknowable. So the question is being run forward instead. Nestlings are being raised within earshot of one dialect only, and will be moved as adults. If they acquire the new trill, storage cannot account for it, and something in the standard description of the learning window will have to give way.

A shell is usually described as armour, and armour is usually described as something that wears out. A crab’s claw punches a hole, the hole stays, and the snail lives or it does not. That description lasted as long as it did partly because shells were mostly studied after the animal inside them had died.

Watching living snails changed it. In tanks where a small puncture was made in the shell of the common dog whelk, the hole closed. passage:
In the records of old observatories there is a puzzle that took a century to settle. A large explosion — a powder store, a quarry blast, a meteor breaking up — would be heard clearly near at hand, then not at all across a broad band of country, and then clearly again far beyond it. The distant listeners were not imagining things; they wrote down the time. One quarry blast, reconstructed afterward from letters, was audible out to fifty-five kilometres, silent from there to a hundred and forty, and plainly heard at a hundred and eighty-seven.

The first explanations looked along the ground, because that is where the listeners were. Wind was blamed, then hills, then the shape of the valleys. None survived a simple objection: the silent band appeared in every direction at once, as a ring around the explosion, and no wind blows outward in all directions from a point.

The answer, when it came, was overhead. Sound bends toward whatever is cooler, and although the air grows colder with height for the first several kilometres, there is a layer much higher in which it grows warmer again. Sound that leaves the ground at a shallow angle climbs into that layer, bends, and comes back down — landing, by then, a long way out. The near listeners hear the sound that never left the ground. The ring of silence is the gap between the two.

One consequence is that a distant bang is a message about air no instrument has been in. Between the wars, before balloons could be sent high enough, the height and warmth of that layer were estimated from nothing but the radius of silence around large explosions: an odd way to measure the sky, and for two decades the only way there was. When balloons at last reached the layer, the figures the explosions had given proved low by about eight percent, an error traced to the assumption that the ground and the layer shared a single wind.

In the records of old observatories there is a puzzle that took a century to settle. A large explosion — a powder store, a quarry blast, a meteor breaking up — would be heard clearly near at hand, then not at all across a broad band of country, and then clearly again far beyond it. The distant listeners were not imagining things; they wrote down the time. One quarry blast, reconstructed afterward from letters, was audible out to fifty-five kilometres, silent from there to a hundred and forty, and plainly heard at a hundred and eighty-seven.

The first explanations looked along the ground, because that is where the listeners were. Wind was blamed, then hills, then the shape of the valleys. None survived a simple objection: the silent band appeared in every direction at once, as a ring around the explosion, and no wind blows outward in all directions from a point.

The answer, when it came, was overhead. Sound bends toward whatever is cooler, and although the air grows colder with height for the first several kilometres, there is a layer much higher in which it grows warmer again. Sound that leaves the ground at a shallow angle climbs into that layer, bends, and comes back down — landing, by then, a long way out. The near listeners hear the sound that never left the ground. The ring of silence is the gap between the two.

One consequence is that a distant bang is a message about air no instrument has been in. Between the wars, before balloons could be sent high enough, the height and warmth of that layer were estimated from nothing but the radius of silence around large explosions: an odd way to measure the sky, and for two decades the only way there was. When balloons at last reached the layer, the figures the explosions had given proved low by about eight percent, an error traced to the assumption that the ground and the layer shared a single wind.

For as long as the famine of that decade has been written about, it has been explained by the weather. Three dry summers in a row, a harvest that failed twice, and a district that lost perhaps a tenth of its people: the chain seems complete, and the chronicles composed soon afterward assert it in almost those words.

The ledgers of the district’s grain houses, catalogued for the first time only recently, do not fit the chain. They show that the stores were not empty. In the worst of the three years the granaries of the market town held enough to feed the district for eleven weeks, and in those same twelve months the town shipped a little over a third of its stock downriver, where prices were higher. Grain left a starving district in daylight, under the seal of the magistrate who was also writing to the capital to ask for relief.

Historians who have read the ledgers divide over what they show. One group reads a failure of authority. The magistrate could have closed the river and did not, and the chronicles that blame the weather were written by men with reason to prefer that explanation. passage:
Ask why people form a line and most will answer that a line is fair: first to arrive, first to be served. The answer is so satisfying that for a long time nobody tested it, and the few researchers who thought about queues at all treated them as a piece of etiquette that some societies had acquired and others had not.

A set of experiments in three transport stations makes fairness look more like a consequence than a cause. The researchers set up two temporary counters, identical except in one respect: at the first, a waiting person could see the clerk and whoever was being served; at the second, a screen hid both. Fairness predicts no difference between them, since the rule about arrival order holds just as well behind a screen. What the researchers observed was that a single file formed at the hidden counter in seventy-one percent of trials and at the visible counter in twenty-four percent. Where the front of the service was in view, people spread into a loose crowd and watched.

The explanation the researchers favour is that a queue is a device for handling uncertainty. A person who cannot see what is happening at the front cannot judge how long the wait will be, and joining a line turns an unanswerable question into a countable one: there are nine people ahead of me. Where the front is visible, that information is already to hand, and the line is not worth the cost of standing in it.

A rival account is simpler and harder to be rid of. People copy what they see. At the hidden counter the first two arrivals had nothing to look at except each other, and a third arrival who finds two people standing one behind another will stand behind them. If that is all it is, the seventy-one percent is a fact about imitation and says nothing about uncertainty. The researchers concede the point. Every arrangement that hides the clerk, they note, also leaves a newcomer with the queue as the only thing worth looking at.

The sea wall that closes the old harbour has been explained the same way for two hundred years: it was thrown up in haste during the war, to keep a hostile fleet out of the anchorage. The explanation fits the wall’s appearance — massive, plain, and finished carelessly at the northern end — and it fits the one document that mentions the wall at all, a council order from the second year of the war directing that the harbour be made safe.

Timbers taken from the wall’s foundation have now been dated by their growth rings, and they were felled eighty years before the war began. That fact does not by itself move the wall. Old timber was valuable and was reused constantly, and a beam cut eighty years earlier might simply have spent those eighty years in a barn or in someone else’s hall. But these timbers were not reused. A reused beam carries the empty joints of its first life, cut for pegs that are no longer there, and these beams carry none. They were felled, shaped, and set into the foundation as one piece of work.

If the wall is eighty years older than the war, the council order cannot be its origin, and the obvious alternative is trade. A wall of that length makes a basin where cargo can be worked in any weather, and the decades before the felling date are the decades in which the town’s shipping tripled.

The argument is good but not airtight, and its weakest joint is the one most easily passed over. Growth rings date the felling of a tree, not the building of a wall. A merchant town whose shipping had tripled might well have squared timber and stacked it against work still to come, and a stacked beam is unused timber with no empty joints — indistinguishable from the case the argument needs. The reasoning holds only if the town kept no timber yard, and on that the record says nothing at all.
